title: Pietro Chierico
text:
Email ORCID ResearchGate LinkedIn GitHub




PhD Student in Biomedical Engineering
I work at the intersection of digital health, physiological signal processing, wearable sensing, and biomedical AI, with a focus on making cardiovascular monitoring technologies more reliable, reproducible, and clinically meaningful.
My research focuses especially on photoplethysmography (PPG), signal quality assessment, beat detection, and AI-based methods for interpreting physiological signals from wearable devices. I am interested in translating robust biomedical engineering methods into real-world digital health applications.
Previously, I gained international research and engineering experience at the University of Illinois Chicago, Politecnico di Milano, NECSTLab, and STMicroelectronics, working across biomedical engineering, embedded technologies, and applied physiological sensing. I also completed a visiting PhD period at Khalifa University (Abu Dhabi), working with Prof. Mohamed Elgendi on wearable PPG sensing and biomedical signal education.

Latest
PulseCraft PPG — an open photoplethysmography teaching kit. Designed and built during my visiting PhD period at Khalifa University for the CMHS Summer Internship Program 2026: five hands-on PPG projects (activity recognition, caffeine response, relaxation biofeedback, an apnea/SpO2 proxy, stress detection), with Arduino/ESP32 firmware, a 3D-printable sensor case, Python feature-extraction and ML pipelines, and a no-hardware signal simulator. title: Research
text:
I develop signal-processing and machine-learning methods for wearable cardiovascular monitoring, with a particular focus on photoplethysmography (PPG).
My work addresses a practical challenge in digital health: how to make physiological signals collected from wearable devices more reliable, interpretable, and useful in real-world biomedical applications.

title: Research
text:
Main research lines



PPG signal quality assessment


I work on methods to identify reliable and unreliable PPG segments in wearable recordings, where motion artifacts, sensor contact, and physiological variability can strongly affect signal interpretation.




Noise-resilient beat detection


I develop and evaluate peak detection methods for PPG signals, with the goal of improving pulse detection under noisy and real-world monitoring conditions.




Wearable cardiovascular monitoring


I am interested in extracting robust cardiovascular information from wearable sensors, including heart rate dynamics, pulse-related features, and clinically meaningful signal descriptors.




Evaluation of biomedical signal pipelines


I study how preprocessing, beat detection, feature extraction, and model design influence the performance of biomedical signal analysis systems.

title: Research
text:
Open-source & teaching


PulseCraft PPG — an open photoplethysmography teaching kit


Designed and built end-to-end during my visiting PhD period at Khalifa University, for the CMHS Summer Internship Program 2026 (Biomedical Engineering & Biotechnology track). Five hands-on PPG projects — activity recognition, caffeine response, relaxation biofeedback, a voluntary-apnea SpO2 proxy, and live stress detection — with Arduino/ESP32 acquisition firmware, a 3D-printable sensor case, Python data-collection and machine-learning pipelines, and a no-hardware signal simulator. Released open-source (MIT / CC BY 4.0) so any lab, course, or individual can build on it.
